titre: Saharan Dust, the Amazon's Fertilizer from a Vanished Lake
accroche: Every year, 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust fall on the Amazon and replace the phosphorus that rain washes away.
contenu_vulgarise:
After strong winds, an ocher cloud rises above the Sahara, stretches out over the Atlantic, and falls on the largest tropical forest in the world. In 2015, a team from NASA and the University of Maryland measured its volume in three dimensions for the first time, from space.

## The Mechanism

The CALIPSO satellite sends pulses of laser light toward the Earth (a lidar), which bounce off particles in the atmosphere. Their optical properties make it possible to tell dust from other aerosols. From 2007 to 2013, the measurements give an average of 182 million tons of dust a year leaving the Sahara to the west, at 15° West longitude. Near the east coast of South America, at 35° West, 132 million tons remain in the air, and 27.7 million tons fall on the Amazon basin. About 43 million tons continue on toward the Caribbean Sea.

This dust matters for what it contains. Part of it comes from the Bodélé Depression in Chad, an ancient lake bed whose rocks are made of dead microorganisms, very rich in phosphorus. Amazonian soils, however, are poor in nutrients: most of it is stored in the plants themselves and recycled by falling leaves. Phosphorus is carried by rain into waterways, and the forest loses it like a slowly leaking bathtub.

The researchers estimate that the dust brings about 22,000 tons of phosphorus a year, roughly what rain and floods take away. The estimate rests on the proportion of phosphorus measured in dust sampled at the Bodélé and at ground stations in Barbados and Miami.

## The Shift

We readily picture the rainforest as a closed system, living off its own humus. That is roughly true for most nutrients, and false for the one that escapes. The phosphorus balance only works out thanks to a desert, and more precisely thanks to a lake that no longer exists: the forest lives in part on the remains of another ecosystem.

The limits are stated in NASA's article. Seven years of data are too short to identify trends, says Chip Trepte, CALIPSO's project scientist, who did not take part in the study. As for phosphorus, it is calculated from the composition of samples, not measured from above. What remains to be seen is what becomes of this transfer as the climate changes: for the lead author, Hongbin Yu, dust acts on the climate, and the climate acts on dust.

repere.texte: CALIPSO, 2007-2013: 182 million tons of dust leave the Sahara each year, 27.7 million tons fall on the Amazon basin, with about 22,000 tons of phosphorus.
repere.source: NASA Goddard, “NASA Satellite Reveals How Much Saharan Dust Feeds Amazon's Plants,” 2015

carte.punch: 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust fall on the Amazon every year.
carte.idee: A NASA satellite quantified in 2015 the dust that crosses the Atlantic: 182 million tons leave the Sahara each year, 27.7 million fall on the Amazon. It brings about 22,000 tons of phosphorus, roughly what the forest loses to rain and floods.

quiz.question: Why does Saharan dust matter for Amazonian soils?
choix: It neutralizes soil acidity and protects tree roots
It forms a layer that holds soil moisture during the dry season
It brings the nitrogen that tropical trees cannot fix on their own
It brings phosphorus, which rain and floods wash out of the forest
quiz.explication: Dust from the Bodélé is rich in phosphorus, a scarce nutrient in Amazonian soils that rain carries off to the rivers: the Saharan input, about 22,000 tons a year, roughly makes up for this loss. The text attributes to it no role in acidity, water retention, or nitrogen supply.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did the NASA team measure the volume of Saharan dust in three dimensions in 2015?
choix: With weather stations set up along the Atlantic
With the lidar of the CALIPSO satellite, which sends laser pulses
By counting grains deposited on plates placed in the Amazon
With visible images from an ordinary weather satellite
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The CALIPSO satellite sends laser pulses that bounce off atmospheric particles; their optical properties distinguish dust from other aerosols. The text mentions no ground stations, plates, or visible imagery for this measurement.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does most of the phosphorus that Saharan dust brings to the Amazon come from?
choix: From recent volcanic ash blown in from East Africa
From agricultural fertilizers carried from the Sahel by the winds
From the Bodélé Depression, an ancient lake bed rich in dead microorganisms
From sand dunes in the central Sahara, rich in minerals
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Bodélé Depression, in Chad, is an ancient lake bed whose rocks are made of dead microorganisms, very rich in phosphorus. The text attributes this input neither to volcanic ash, nor to fertilizers, nor to the dunes of the central Sahara.
